svg.text: The fixed algorithm is a family
Council Regulation (EC) No 1103/97, Art. 4 and 5, measured on the eleven irrevocably fixed rates of Reg. (EC) No 2866/98.
Exact integer arithmetic throughout; every value below is recomputable from convert.py → data.json.
A. The apparatus Art. 4(3) forbids by name, and the one the reason for the ban actually reaches
amount converted, in minor units of the national currency (log scale)
share of amounts on which the banned result
differs from the one the statute requires
the same inverse as a float64:
Recital (10) grounds the ban on accuracy — inverse rates “could result in significant inaccuracies, notably if large amounts are involved”. True of the six-figure inverse,
though the first single-unit divergence already appears at 30.86 BEF — €0.76 — and turns systematic from about €2,608 upward.
But Art. 4(3) bans “inverse rates” without qualification, so it equally bans the float64 inverse, which never diverges anywhere in the scan. The prohibition outlives its reason.
B. The methods Art. 4(4) permits, disagreeing with each other
each of the 108 ordered currency pairs, ranked — all 108 of them disagree
Rounding the intermediate euro amount to three decimals, to four, five, six, or not at all: the first clause of Art. 4(4) permits all five.
On amounts up to 4,000 minor units they spread by as much as 3 minor units. The second clause of the very same sentence reads:
“No alternative method of calculation may be used unless it produces the same results.”
C. The exact half-way amounts, where no measurement can prefer either side
statute and machine return different money
a tie both rules happen to resolve the same way
Tall marks: the statute (Art. 5, “the sum shall be rounded up”) and the prevailing machine default (round half to even) return different money — exactly half of all ties.
€1500.00 is exactly 2933.745 German marks. The statute says 2933.75, IEEE 754-2019’s default rounding attribute says 2933.74. Neither is nearer.
